impacts.caseName: Teva Pharmaceuticals International GmbH v. Eli Lilly and Company
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the enablement requirement under 35 U.S.C. § 112 for broad method claims reciting a genus of antibodies requires the same full-scope analysis applied to composition claims, particularly after Amgen v. Sanofi.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit denied en banc rehearing of a panel decision upholding broad method claims for treating headache using anti-CGRP antagonist antibodies, despite a vigorous dissent arguing the panel's enablement standard for method claims conflicts with Supreme Court precedent and will sustain overly broad claims. The dissent warned the decision undermines medical innovation by allowing functionally defined genus claims without adequate enablement scrutiny.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders with broad method-of-treatment claims benefit from a potentially more lenient enablement standard for method claims compared to composition claims, preserving broader patent scope for biologics and pharmaceutical inventions.
impacts.negativeImplications: Competitors and generic/biosimilar manufacturers face broader blocking patents on therapeutic methods, as the decision may allow patentees to claim entire genera of antibodies for treatment methods without enabling the full scope of the genus.

impacts.caseName: Dental Monitoring SAS v. Align Technology, Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether, under AIA 35 U.S.C. § 102(d)(2), a reference patent can rely on a provisional application's filing date as its effective prior art date without requiring that at least one claim of the non-provisional patent be supported by the provisional's written description, as required under pre-AIA law by Dynamic Drinkware.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated a PTAB decision finding dental imaging patent claims obvious, addressing whether the Board's Penumbra framework—which relaxed the Dynamic Drinkware written description requirement for determining a reference's prior art date under the AIA—was properly applied. The court remanded for further consideration of the applicable standard for establishing a reference patent's effective prior art date under AIA § 102(d)(2).
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent owners may benefit if the court ultimately requires stricter written description support for provisional-based prior art dates, narrowing the pool of prior art available to challengers in IPR proceedings.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies relying on IPR challenges face uncertainty about what standard applies to establish a reference's prior art date through provisional applications under the AIA, potentially complicating invalidity arguments.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether an exclusive license agreement conveyed 'all substantial rights' in the patents to the licensee, entitling it to sue for infringement without joining the patent owner, and whether the licensee's shift to an enforcement-only business model triggered an automatic termination clause.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's dismissal of TexasLDPC's patent infringement suit against Broadcom, holding that the exclusive license from Texas A&M University conveyed all substantial rights and that TexasLDPC's transition to enforcement-only operations did not constitute a cessation of business triggering automatic license termination. The court found TexasLDPC had standing to sue without joining A&M.
impacts.positiveImplications: Exclusive licensees and patent assertion entities benefit from confirmation that shifting to an enforcement-focused business model does not automatically terminate license agreements, and that exclusive licenses conveying all substantial rights confer standing to sue independently.
impacts.negativeImplications: Accused infringers lose the ability to challenge standing based on a licensee's shift to enforcement-only operations, potentially facing more lawsuits from patent assertion entities holding exclusive licenses from universities.

impacts.caseName: Versata Software, LLC v. Ford Motor Company
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court erred in excluding plaintiff's trade secret damages expert and whether the jury's breach of contract damages award should be reinstated.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the trade secret damages judgment and remanded for a new trial, instructing the district court to reconsider two previously rejected damages models. The court also reversed the district court's judgment on breach of contract damages and reinstated the jury's award. The court affirmed Ford's liability for trade secret misappropriation under both the DTSA and Michigan law.
impacts.positiveImplications: Software developers and licensors benefit from the reinstatement of jury damages awards for breach of contract and the expanded opportunity to present alternative damages theories for trade secret misappropriation.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies that develop internal replacements for licensed software face significant trade secret misappropriation liability, with courts now required to more carefully consider multiple damages models rather than excluding expert testimony.

impacts.caseName: Constellation Designs, LLC v. LG Electronics Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patent claims directed to non-uniform constellations for digital communications are patent-eligible under 35 U.S.C. § 101, and whether the district court properly sustained a jury verdict of willful infringement and damages.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit issued a mixed ruling, vacating the summary judgment of patent eligibility for some asserted claims while affirming eligibility for others, and affirming the jury's infringement and damages findings. The decision provides important guidance on the Alice/Mayo framework as applied to communications technology patents, distinguishing between claims that recite abstract mathematical concepts and those tied to specific technological implementations.
impacts.positiveImplications: Technology companies holding patents on specific implementations of mathematical or algorithmic innovations in communications systems receive support for eligibility of claims tied to concrete technological improvements.
impacts.negativeImplications: Consumer electronics manufacturers face continued exposure to patent infringement suits on communications standard technology, with the court affirming that implementation-specific claims in this space survive § 101 challenges.

impacts.caseName: Range of Motion Products, LLC v. Armaid Company Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the Egyptian Goddess en banc framework for design patent infringement improperly focuses on differences rather than overall similarity, and whether functionality determinations in design patent claim construction present factual questions for the jury.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit denied en banc rehearing in a design patent case, with a concurrence defending the Egyptian Goddess framework and a dissent (joined by multiple judges) arguing the framework has been misapplied to improperly focus on differences rather than overall similarity, enabling premature summary judgment dispositions without adequate consideration of prior art. The split highlights ongoing tension in design patent infringement law.
impacts.positiveImplications: Design patent defendants benefit from the continued application of the Egyptian Goddess standard, which permits summary judgment of non-infringement when claimed and accused designs are sufficiently distinct.
impacts.negativeImplications: Design patent holders face a heightened risk of summary judgment against them, as the dissent highlighted concerns that courts are too readily finding non-infringement by focusing on differences rather than overall visual impression, and the four dissenting judges signal potential for future en banc reconsideration.

impacts.caseName: Epic Tech, LLC v. Pen-Tech Associates, Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a district court must provide sufficient detail in denying motions for Rule 11 sanctions and attorneys' fees under 35 U.S.C. § 285 where the patentee continued to assert patent claims after related claims were rejected under § 101 and a related patent was invalidated.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated and remanded the district court's denial of sanctions and fees motions, holding the court's order lacked sufficient detail for meaningful appellate review. The case involved a patent assertion where related applications had been rejected under § 101 post-Alice and the patentee had abandoned those applications without overcoming the rejections, raising questions about whether the infringement suit was exceptional under § 285.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers benefit from the requirement that district courts provide detailed reasoning when denying fee-shifting motions, particularly where there are strong indicators that the asserted patent may be invalid under § 101.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent assertion entities face increased risk of fee awards where they assert patents with claims closely related to those previously rejected or invalidated under § 101, as courts must now more carefully analyze and explain their fee decisions.

impacts.caseName: VDPP, LLC v. Volkswagen Group of America, Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a district court properly awarded attorneys' fees under 35 U.S.C. § 285 and sanctioned plaintiff's counsel under 28 U.S.C. § 1927 for filing a frivolous patent infringement action, and whether dismissal without leave to amend was proper.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the dismissal of a patent infringement complaint without leave to amend, upheld the § 285 attorneys' fees award against the plaintiff, and addressed counsel sanctions. The court found the proposed amended complaint was futile and that the plaintiff had implicitly agreed not to amend in exchange for a filing extension. The decision reinforces accountability for patent plaintiffs who file insufficiently pleaded infringement claims.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers benefit from strong enforcement of fee-shifting provisions against frivolous patent suits, with courts willing to award both § 285 fees and § 1927 sanctions where infringement claims are inadequately supported.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent plaintiffs and their counsel face significant financial exposure for filing infringement suits with insufficient factual basis, particularly where they fail to adequately plead pre-suit damages theories.

impacts.caseName: T-Mobile US, Inc. v. KAIFI LLC
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Circuit has jurisdiction over a dispute concerning the interpretation of a patent litigation settlement agreement's contingent payment clause tied to ex parte reexamination outcomes.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit held it lacked subject-matter jurisdiction over a dispute about whether T-Mobile owed an additional settlement payment contingent on patent claims 'surviving' an ex parte reexamination, because the dispute was fundamentally a contract interpretation question governed by state law rather than a substantial patent law question. The court transferred the case to the Fifth Circuit.
impacts.positiveImplications: Parties to patent settlements benefit from clarity that contract disputes over settlement terms will be resolved under state contract law in regional circuits rather than the Federal Circuit, potentially providing more predictable contract interpretation standards.
impacts.negativeImplications: Parties who structured settlement agreements around patent proceedings may face unexpected jurisdictional complications, as disputes over settlement terms tied to PTO outcomes may not be heard by the Federal Circuit despite their patent nexus.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether Commerce's regulation requiring domestic interested parties to indicate intent to participate in an antidumping sunset review within 15 days of initiation conflicts with the governing statute, which is silent on filing deadlines.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the Court of International Trade and upheld Commerce's 15-day participation deadline regulation for antidumping sunset reviews, finding the statute was silent on timing and the regulation represented a permissible exercise of the agency's delegated authority through reasoned decisionmaking. The decision reinstates Commerce's procedural framework for sunset review participation.
impacts.positiveImplications: Domestic manufacturers benefit from a clear, enforceable deadline that ensures prompt initiation of sunset review proceedings, supporting the continuation of antidumping duty orders that protect against unfairly priced imports.
impacts.negativeImplications: Importers and foreign producers face a strict 15-day window to respond to sunset review notices, and domestic parties who miss the deadline risk automatic revocation of protective antidumping orders.

impacts.caseName: Satius Holding, LLC v. Samsung Electronics Co., Ltd.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patent claims directed to a communications apparatus for transmitting signals 'over air' are indefinite and whether they satisfy the enablement requirement of 35 U.S.C. § 112(a).
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed invalidity of communications apparatus patent claims asserted against Samsung, reversing the district court's indefiniteness ruling but affirming on the alternative ground of lack of enablement. The court held that while the claims were not indefinite, they failed to enable the full scope of the claimed invention, providing guidance on the interplay between indefiniteness and enablement defenses.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers benefit from the court's willingness to affirm invalidity on alternative grounds, and the decision reinforces that overly broad functional claims in electronics patents remain vulnerable to enablement challenges.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders with broad communications technology claims face heightened enablement scrutiny, particularly where claims encompass physical phenomena that the specification does not adequately teach how to achieve across the full claimed scope.

impacts.caseName: Exelixis, Inc. v. MSN Laboratories Private Ltd.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patent claims directed to crystalline and amorphous forms of cabozantinib (L)-malate salts satisfy the written description requirement of 35 U.S.C. § 112(a) when the specification describes specific crystalline polymorphs but does not separately characterize the amorphous form.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the district court's finding that Exelixis's malate salt patents had adequate written description for claims covering both crystalline and amorphous forms of the cancer drug cabozantinib. The decision is significant for pharmaceutical patent litigation as it addresses the scope of written description support needed for claims covering different solid forms of an active pharmaceutical ingredient.
impacts.positiveImplications: Pharmaceutical patent holders benefit from the court's recognition that written description for salt form claims does not necessarily require separate characterization of every physical form, supporting broader patent protection for drug formulations.
impacts.negativeImplications: Generic pharmaceutical companies face stronger patent barriers to market entry, as the decision supports broader written description coverage for drug substance patents that claim multiple physical forms without individually describing each.
